traits.name: Tail risk blindness
traits.now: Just three trades account for 87% of everything you lost.
traits.why: Most trades feel controlled, so risk feels controlled. But the damage is concentrated in a few moments when discipline slipped. Those few trades decide the year, and they are the ones that never get reviewed.
traits.ideal: No single trade can lose more than a fixed cash amount, set before entry. The worst trades get reviewed first.

traits.name: The one-big-loss problem
traits.now: Your worst trade lost €631.9K, about 14 average wins.
traits.why: A single large loss usually starts as a normal trade that was never stopped out. Each small move against you felt too small to act on, until the total was too big to accept.
traits.ideal: The maximum loss on any trade is about one average win. Anything bigger is treated as a process failure, not bad luck.

traits.name: Inconsistent sizing
traits.now: Your position sizes vary wildly: the spread is 3.5× the average size.
traits.why: When size is decided by feel, conviction and mood set the bet. Your biggest positions end up where you felt most certain, which is not the same as where your edge is greatest.
traits.ideal: Position size comes from a formula: risk per trade divided by distance to stop.

traits.name: Tilt
traits.now: Your longest losing run was 7 trades in a row, costing €1,771.11.
traits.why: After several losses, frustration takes over decision-making. Each new loss lowers the bar for the next entry, until trading becomes a way to vent rather than a process.
traits.ideal: A daily loss limit and a maximum number of consecutive losses, after which trading stops for the day.

traits.name: Day-level spirals
traits.now: Your worst day (2025-03-21) lost €631.9K across 1 trades.
traits.why: Bad days rarely start bad. A normal loss is followed by a push to recover, then a bigger push. By the end of the day, one mistake has become several.
traits.ideal: A daily loss limit that ends the session. Tomorrow is a fresh start.

traits.name: Risk drift
traits.now: Your first half of trades made €801.4K; the second half lost €416.0K.
traits.why: Early success often leads to quietly larger risk, looser selection and more trades. The rules that produced the gains erode one small exception at a time.
traits.ideal: The rules that produced good results are written down and reviewed weekly, so they don't drift.

traits.name: Weekday blind spot
traits.now: Friday is your worst day: 10 trades, 30% win rate, −€661.3K.
traits.why: Patterns tied to a day of the week are often about you, not the market: energy levels, routines, expiries, or what happened the day before.
traits.ideal: Days that consistently lose get smaller size or no trading until the reason is understood.

traits.name: Emotional bankroll
traits.now: You gave back a large share of your peak profit by the end of the period.
traits.why: Giving back gains is hard to accept, so trading continues more aggressively to recover the peak. The peak becomes an anchor, and chasing it deepens the drawdown.
traits.ideal: A drawdown limit from the peak. Hitting it triggers a reduction in size and a review.

more.name: Moving the goalposts
more.now: 13 positions lost more than half their value before being closed.
more.why: A stop that exists only in your head is easy to move. Each time price reaches it, a new reason appears for giving the trade more room, and the planned small loss becomes a large one.
more.ideal: Stops are placed with the broker at entry, so moving them requires a deliberate, visible action.

more.name: Volatility denial
more.now: 4 futures positions lost 5% or more of notional value.
more.why: Leverage hides risk. A 5% move feels small in percentage terms, but on a futures position it can equal weeks of gains. The brain judges the move, not the exposure.
more.ideal: Futures risk is measured in cash per lot. The stop is set so a full stop-out is a normal, survivable loss.

more.name: Chasing the same name
more.now: 4 times you re-entered the same name on the same day you lost on it, losing €98.2K more.
more.why: Losing on a specific stock or contract makes it personal. Re-entering is an attempt to win back from that particular instrument, as if it owed you something.
more.ideal: After a loss on a name, that name is off-limits for the rest of the day.

more.name: Drawdown denial
more.now: At the worst point you were €668.6K below your peak.
more.why: A deep drawdown is easy to dismiss as temporary. But the depth of a drawdown shows how much risk was really being taken, regardless of where the account ends up.
more.ideal: A maximum drawdown is set in advance. Reaching it means stopping and reassessing.

more.name: Friday restlessness
more.why: The end of the week brings a push to finish the week green or make one more trade before the weekend. Rushed trades follow.
more.ideal: Weekly goals are not chased on Friday. A red week is accepted rather than forced green.

more.name: Calendar fixation
more.now: Your best weekday (Tuesday) and worst (Friday) differ by €1.37M.
more.why: Large differences between days point to routine and mindset rather than market structure. Your best day shows how you trade when conditions suit you.
more.ideal: Recreate the conditions of your best day (preparation, timing, mood) on the others.

more.name: Self-attribution after streaks
more.now: You had a 5-trade winning streak and a 7-trade losing streak.
more.why: Winning streaks feel like skill and losing streaks feel like bad luck. Both are often the same process meeting different market conditions.
more.ideal: Size and rules stay the same through streaks of either kind.

more.name: Learning blind spot
more.now: Your biggest losses are concentrated in a few trades that are easy to forget.
more.why: Painful trades are the ones we least want to look at, so they get the least review. They are also the ones with the most to teach.
more.ideal: Review the three worst trades of every month before anything else.

more.name: Unexamined winners
more.now: You're profitable overall, but a few losses still do most of the damage.
more.why: When the total is positive, there's little urge to look closer. But the few large losses show where the next big setback will come from.
more.ideal: Even in good periods, review the largest losses and what allowed them.

net.ideal: Net P&L after costs is the only number that pays. Judge every change to your trading by its effect here.

gross.ideal: Gross P&L should comfortably exceed costs; if it barely does, trade less, not more.

costs.now: Costs were 0% of what your winners made.
costs.ideal: Costs under 15–20% of gross profit. Fewer trades with larger targets get you there.

winrate.ideal: Win rate only matters alongside payoff. 40% with 2:1 winners beats 60% with 1:2.

payoff.now: Average win is 1.54× the average loss.
payoff.ideal: A payoff above 1.5 gives room for a normal win rate to be profitable.

avgwin.ideal: Winners run to a planned target instead of being taken at the first sign of profit.

avgloss.ideal: Losers closed at a pre-set stop, so the average loss is smaller than the average win.

pf.ideal: A profit factor above 1.3 after costs is a sustainable edge.

worst.now: Your worst trade was €631.9K, about 13.9 average wins.
worst.ideal: The worst trade is no bigger than one or two average wins.

costsPanel.ideal: Every trade expected to make several times its cost.

leaks.ideal: Leaks are fixed one at a time, starting with the most expensive.

curve.now: At the worst point you were €668.6K below your peak.
curve.ideal: A steady upward slope with shallow dips; deep drops mean risk per trade is too high.

instrument.ideal: Capital goes to the instrument where your results are best, not where the action is.

year.ideal: Improvement shows as each year being better than the last.

afterwinloss.now: After a loss your next trade averages €9,633.7; after a win, €3,236.85.
afterwinloss.ideal: The trade after a loss looks like any other trade: same size, same checklist.

diagnosis.ideal: A positive average trade after costs, held steady over hundreds of trades.

rules.now: Rules built from your own mistakes.
rules.ideal: Rules are followed before every trade, not just read once.

patterns.ideal: Do more of what works, pause what consistently doesn't.

psych.ideal: Awareness first; then one rule per habit, tested for a month.

stopsOpt.now: How a premium stop would have changed results.
stopsOpt.ideal: Bought options exit at a fixed share of premium, usually 30–40% down.

stopsLin.ideal: Stops sized so a full stop-out is a normal loss.

working.ideal: Protect your strengths: give them the most capital and the least interference.

group.ideal: Concentrate on the instrument with the best results per trade.

weekday.now: Results by the weekday your contracts expired.
weekday.ideal: If one expiry day stands out as losing, avoid holding into it.

premium.now: Results by the premium you paid.
premium.ideal: Pick strikes for probability and liquidity, not price.

expiryType.ideal: Match the expiry to how long your idea needs.

callPut.ideal: Trade the side the setup shows; review each side separately.

entryDow.now: Friday is your weakest entry day.
entryDow.ideal: Size down on days that consistently lose until you know why.

entryHour.ideal: Trade the hours where your record is best; sit out the rest.

hold.ideal: Winners held at least as long as losers.

busyDay.ideal: A daily trade limit. Quality drops as the count rises.

direction.ideal: Both sides traded when the setup is there.

month.ideal: Most months profitable, with small losing months.

size.ideal: Size follows a formula, not conviction.

style.ideal: Holding period decided at entry, never changed because a trade is losing.

lossDepth.ideal: Most losses small, almost none deep. Deep losses mean stops weren't used.

worstU.now: The names that cost you most.
worstU.ideal: Repeat losers go on a pause list.

bestU.now: The names that pay you most.
bestU.ideal: Give your best names priority and patience.

positions.ideal: Review the worst five positions every week.
